# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 31 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 31 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_031_page_001.jpg

---

## Mandate 4, Chapter 1 — Chastity and Remarriage

**1** "Here is my command to you," he said. "Guard your sexual purity. Don't let any thought about another man's wife enter your heart — no fantasizing about fornication or any of that wickedness. If you do these things, you commit a serious sin. But keep your mind fixed on your own wife, and you will never sin. **2** The moment this kind of desire takes root in your heart, you have sinned. And other things just as bad will follow. For a servant of God, this desire is a grievous sin. Whoever does this wicked thing is working toward his own death. So cut this desire out — because where holiness lives, lawlessness has no business entering the heart of a righteous person." **3** "May I ask you something, sir?" "Ask anything," he said. "Sir, if a man is married to a believing woman and he catches her in adultery — does he sin if he stays with her?" **4** "While he doesn't know about it, he doesn't sin," the Shepherd said. "But once he knows she has sinned and she won't repent — if she keeps on in her adultery and he stays — then he becomes complicit in her sin and shares in her adultery." **5** "So what should he do if she won't stop?" "He must separate from her and stay single. But if he leaves her and remarries, he commits adultery himself." **6** "But what if, after the separation, she changes her mind and repents and wants to come back? Shouldn't he take her back?" **7** "Yes, absolutely. If he refuses to take her back, he sins greatly. The one who has sinned and repented must be welcomed back — though not again and again and again. Because for God's servants there is only one repentance. On account of that possibility of repentance, the husband shouldn't remarry. And this applies equally to wives too."

---

*PNEUMA note: The asymmetry-breaking final line — "this applies equally to wives too" — is notable. The Shepherd explicitly applies the same rule to women that it applied to men, which is unusual for its time.*
